schema_note: P7 region evidence. One verbatim quote from one paper per row. See README.md.
status: AI-drafted, then checked by a second AI verifier and corrected. No neuroscientist or clinician has reviewed these rows. Research summaries, not medical advice.
display_rule: Show every row as: filed under <filed_under>; the paper says <anatomy_as_stated>. Where anatomy_match is not 'equal' or anatomy_inferred is true, never show the row under the bare region name.

rows.claim: In a lesion study comparing 19 patients with dorsolateral prefrontal lesions, 152 with lesions elsewhere and 54 people without lesions, dorsolateral prefrontal damage was associated with deficits in manipulating verbal and spatial information.
rows.quote: DlPFC damage was associated with deficits in the manipulation of verbal and spatial knowledge
rows.citation: Barbey et al. (2013). Dorsolateral prefrontal contributions to human working memory. Cortex.
rows.study_design: lesion study, three groups compared on standard memory and intelligence subtests and an N-back task
rows.scope_note: Group result, not individual prediction. Covers the dorsolateral part only and working-memory manipulation only; says nothing about personality, planning or social behaviour. Lesion cause and chronicity are not in the abstract.
rows.anatomy_note: part: the paper says 'dorsolateral PFC (dlPFC)'; the QIF region is the whole prefrontal cortex.

rows.claim: In a single-centre series of 25 patients admitted with isolated hand palsy of central origin, an isolated infarct in the hand knob region was found in 18; the other 7 had multiple acute infarctions.
rows.quote: Isolated infarct in the hand knob region was found in 18 of the 25 cases, whereas 7 had multiple acute infarctions.
rows.citation: Orosz et al. (2018). Cortical Hand Knob Stroke: Report of 25 Cases. J Stroke Cerebrovasc Dis.
rows.study_design: retrospective single-centre case series, 2006 to 2016, lesions shown on CT or MRI
rows.scope_note: One centre. Patients were selected because they had hand palsy, so the series cannot say how often a lesion here produces the deficit. The abstract reports quick improvement in almost every case, so it does not support a permanent deficit. The link from 'hand knob' to the precentral gyrus comes from a different paper (Yousry et al. 1997, PMID 9055804), not from the abstract quoted; show this filing as inferred.
rows.anatomy_as_stated: hand knob region; cortical hand knob territory
rows.anatomy_note: part, by the drafter's inference: the abstract says 'cortical hand knob territory' and 'hand knob region' and does not use the words primary motor cortex or precentral gyrus. A reviewer must confirm that the hand knob is the hand area of the precentral gyrus before this row is shown under M1.

related_sources.citation: Yousry et al. (1997). Localization of the motor hand area to a knob on the precentral gyrus. A new landmark. Brain.
related_sources.relation: supports the anatomical link, from a different paper
related_sources.quote: The segment of the precentral gyrus that most often contained motor hand function was a knob-like structure

rows.claim: Two comparison patients with small precentral gyrus lesions had proximal hemiparesis without limb-kinetic apraxia.
rows.quote: Two patients with proximal hemiparesis and small lesions in the precentral gyrus which have been examined for comparison showed no limb-kinetic apraxia and different distributions of the paretic shoulder girdle muscles.
rows.citation: Freund and Hummelsheim (1985). Lesions of premotor cortex in man. Brain.
rows.study_design: case series of frontal lesions on CT; these two patients were a comparison group
rows.scope_note: Two patients, 1985 CT localisation. Describes weakness in these two cases only; says nothing about hemiplegia, the homunculus or recovery.
rows.anatomy_note: equal or part: the paper says 'small lesions in the precentral gyrus' and elsewhere 'primary motor cortex'.

rows.claim: In one 52-year-old blind patient, electrical stimulation through electrodes on the occipital pole of the right hemisphere was associated with sensations of light in the left half of the visual field.
rows.quote: By giving appropriate radio signals, the patient can be caused to experience sensations of light (;phosphenes') in the left half of the visual field.
rows.citation: Brindley and Lewin (1968). The sensations produced by electrical stimulation of the visual cortex. J Physiol.
rows.study_design: single-patient implant study, cortical surface stimulation
rows.scope_note: One patient, 1968. Surface electrodes over the occipital pole; the abstract does not say the stimulated tissue was striate cortex alone. Says nothing about edge, orientation or colour processing. The quote reproduces the punctuation of the PubMed record exactly.
rows.anatomy_as_stated: occipital pole of the right cerebral hemisphere; visual cortex
rows.anatomy_note: larger or overlapping: the paper says 'occipital pole of the right cerebral hemisphere' and 'visual cortex'; the QIF region is primary visual (striate) cortex.

rows.claim: A review of perimetry and imaging in a series of patients with striate cortex disease supported a revised map in which central vision takes a larger share of striate cortex than the older Holmes map gave it.
rows.quote: This study reviews the perimetric and imaging findings in a larger series of patients with striate cortical disease and provides support for the revised representation.
rows.citation: McFadzean et al. (1994). Representation of the visual field in the occipital striate cortex. Br J Ophthalmol.
rows.study_design: clinical and imaging case series; number of patients not in the abstract
rows.scope_note: The abstract gives no sample size and no individual results. It concerns where the visual field maps onto striate cortex, not the term cortical blindness, and it does not address agnosia or optic ataxia.
rows.anatomy_note: equal: the paper says 'striate cortex' and 'striate cortical disease'.

rows.claim: A narrative review with four case studies describes central deafness as rare and as typically associated with bilateral damage to the central auditory system, more probably the closer the bilateral lesions lie to the auditory cortex.
rows.quote: Central deafness is a rare condition typically resulting from bilateral compromise of the CANS. The closer to the auditory cortex bilateral lesions are located, the greater the probability of CD.
rows.citation: Musiek et al. (2019). Central deafness: a review of past and current perspectives. Int J Audiol.
rows.study_design: narrative literature review with four illustrative cases
rows.scope_note: Narrative review, not a systematic one. It concerns bilateral lesions of the central auditory nervous system as a whole; it does not say that damage confined to primary auditory cortex produces deafness, and it does not address unilateral lesions or tinnitus mechanisms.
rows.anatomy_as_stated: central auditory nervous system (CANS); auditory cortex
rows.anatomy_note: larger: the paper says 'central auditory nervous system (CANS)' and 'auditory cortex'; the QIF region is primary auditory cortex only.

rows.claim: From 20 documented cases plus a review of autopsy records and published cases, the authors' findings suggest that infarction of Broca's area and its immediate surroundings causes a mutism that gives way to rapidly improving effortful articulation, with no significant lasting disturbance of language.
rows.quote: The findings suggest that infarction affecting the Broca area and its immediate environs, even deep into the brain, causes a mutism that is replaced by rapidly improving dyspraxic and effortful articulation, but that no significant distrubance in language function persists
rows.citation: Mohr et al. (1978). Broca aphasia: pathologic and clinical. Neurology.
rows.study_design: clinicopathological case series (20 cases by autopsy, CT or arteriogram) with a review of autopsy records and published cases
rows.scope_note: 1978 series with mixed lesion documentation. The paper's own point is that the lasting syndrome called Broca aphasia goes with a much larger infarct, so this row does not support 'damage to Broca's area produces Broca's aphasia'. The misspelling 'distrubance' is in the PubMed record.
rows.anatomy_as_stated: the Broca area and its immediate environs
rows.anatomy_note: equal or slightly larger: the paper says 'the Broca area and its immediate environs'.

rows.claim: In 72 patients with primary progressive aphasia, neuronal loss in temporoparietal areas traditionally counted as Wernicke's area was associated with intact single-word comprehension and inconsistent impairment of sentence comprehension.
rows.quote: neuronal loss in temporoparietal areas, traditionally included within Wernicke's area, leave single word comprehension intact and cause inconsistent impairments of sentence comprehension
rows.citation: Mesulam et al. (2015). The Wernicke conundrum and the anatomy of language comprehension in primary progressive aphasia. Brain.
rows.study_design: clinico-anatomical correlation of cortical atrophy and language scores in primary progressive aphasia
rows.scope_note: CONTESTED TOPIC, recorded and not resolved. The population is neurodegenerative, not stroke; the authors themselves say reports of combined word and sentence comprehension loss come almost exclusively from stroke patients with white-matter damage. The abstract opens by saying the location of Wernicke's area 'remains controversial'. Both rows first filed under this region argue against the classical account; the row from Hillis et al. 2001 gives the classical side.
rows.anatomy_as_stated: temporoparietal areas, traditionally included within Wernicke's area
rows.anatomy_note: equal by label, uncertain by extent: the paper says 'temporoparietal areas, traditionally included within Wernicke's area'.

rows.claim: A review of lesion and imaging data reports that focal damage to the left posterior superior temporal gyrus and adjacent supramarginal gyrus is associated with phonemic paraphasia without impaired word comprehension.
rows.quote: Focal damage to this region produces phonemic paraphasia without impairing word comprehension, i.e., conduction aphasia.
rows.citation: Binder (2017). Current Controversies on Wernicke's Area and its Role in Language. Curr Neurol Neurosci Rep.
rows.study_design: narrative review
rows.scope_note: CONTESTED TOPIC, recorded and not resolved. One author's review; it argues against the classical account, which this file does not source. It also bears on the conduction aphasia dispute noted in the Hodos audit (arcuate fasciculus versus cortex); that dispute is not settled here. Both rows first filed under this region argue against the classical account; the row from Hillis et al. 2001 gives the classical side.
rows.anatomy_as_stated: left posterior superior temporal gyrus and adjacent supramarginal gyrus
rows.anatomy_note: equal by the paper's own definition: 'the left posterior superior temporal gyrus and adjacent supramarginal gyrus', which it says is what the label Wernicke's area is usually applied to.

rows.claim: In 11 patients with frontal lesions lying in front of the precentral gyrus, moderate weakness of shoulder and hip muscles and limb-kinetic apraxia were observed on the side opposite the lesion.
rows.quote: Moderate unilateral weakness of shoulder and hip muscles and limb-kinetic apraxia were observed in 11 patients with frontal lobe lesions on the side opposite to the neurological deficits.
rows.citation: Freund and Hummelsheim (1985). Lesions of premotor cortex in man. Brain.
rows.study_design: case series, lesions localised on CT (9 infarcts, 2 tumours; 1 purely subcortical)
rows.scope_note: Eleven patients, 1985 CT localisation, one lesion purely subcortical. The apraxia named is limb-kinetic, not ideomotor. Says nothing about mirror neurons or autism.
rows.anatomy_note: equal: the paper says the lesions were 'involving the premotor cortex but not the primary motor cortex'.

rows.claim: In a prospective series of 28 patients having surgery that involved the supplementary motor area, 25 had new aphasia and/or hemiparesis immediately afterwards, to a degree that depended on how much of the area was resected.
rows.quote: Immediately after surgery, 25 (89%) of the 28 patients displayed additional neurological deficits (aphasia and/or hemiparesis) that depended on the extent of the SMA resection.
rows.citation: Zentner et al. (1996). Functional results after resective procedures involving the supplementary motor area. J Neurosurg.
rows.study_design: prospective surgical series, resection for tumour (19) or non-tumour lesions (9)
rows.scope_note: One centre. Patients already had lesions and most had seizures. The deficits reported are aphasia and hemiparesis; the abstract does not use the terms motor neglect or alien hand. Read with the companion row on recovery.
rows.anatomy_note: equal: the paper says 'supplementary motor area (SMA)'.

rows.claim: In the same series of 28 patients, the deficits after supplementary motor area resection resolved within 3 to 42 days, apart from a minimal disturbance of fine motor or speech function in complex or fast tasks.
rows.quote: Neurological disorders resolved completely within 3 to 42 days (mean 11 days), except for a minimal disturbance of fine motor and/or speech function in complex tasks or at high speed.
rows.citation: Zentner et al. (1996). Functional results after resective procedures involving the supplementary motor area. J Neurosurg.
rows.study_design: prospective surgical series, resection for tumour (19) or non-tumour lesions (9)
rows.scope_note: One centre, unilateral resections only. Does not describe bilateral damage.
rows.anatomy_note: equal: the paper says 'supplementary motor area (SMA)'.

rows.claim: In a lesion-mapping study of 35 patients with right-hemisphere stroke, all of those who had neglect after a middle cerebral artery stroke had damage involving the angular gyrus of the inferior parietal lobe; the abstract does not give their number, and the paper says the critical site is intensely disputed.
rows.quote: For patients with MCA territory strokes, the critical area involved in all neglect patients was the angular gyrus of the inferior parietal lobe (IPL).
rows.citation: Mort et al. (2003). The anatomy of visual neglect. Brain.
rows.study_design: lesion mapping on high-resolution MRI in right-hemisphere stroke patients with and without neglect
rows.scope_note: CONTESTED TOPIC: the abstract's first sentence says the regions critically associated with neglect 'have become intensely disputed', and this paper argues against a rival claim for the superior temporal gyrus. The same paper associates neglect after posterior cerebral artery stroke with the parahippocampal region, outside the parietal lobe. The Hodos audit lists white-matter accounts as well. Group result. The rival claim is Karnath et al. 2001 (PMID 11418859), filed as its own row under this region.
rows.anatomy_as_stated: angular gyrus of the inferior parietal lobe (IPL)
rows.anatomy_note: part: the paper says 'angular gyrus of the inferior parietal lobe (IPL)'; the QIF region is the whole posterior parietal cortex.

rows.claim: In a group of unilateral stroke patients with optic ataxia, the area of lesion overlap lay at the occipito-parietal junction on the lateral surface, in both hemispheres, and not centred on the superior parietal lobule.
rows.quote: In both left and right hemispheres, we found optic ataxia associated with a lesion overlap that affected the lateral cortical convexity at the occipito-parietal junction
rows.citation: Karnath and Perenin (2005). Cortical control of visually guided reaching: evidence from patients with optic ataxia. Cereb Cortex.
rows.study_design: lesion overlap analysis in unilateral stroke patients collected over 15 years; number not in the abstract
rows.scope_note: Sample size is not in the abstract. The overlap is at the border of parietal and occipital cortex and extends to the precuneus, so it supports 'parieto-occipital junction', not 'posterior parietal cortex' as a whole. Group overlap, not individual prediction.
rows.anatomy_as_stated: occipito-parietal junction; precuneus close to the occipito-parietal junction
rows.anatomy_note: part and partly outside: the paper says 'the junction between the inferior parietal lobule (IPL) and superior occipital cortex' and the 'precuneus close to the occipito-parietal junction'.

rows.claim: In one person with long-term spinal cord injury, microstimulation in the hand area of somatosensory cortex was associated with tactile sensations felt as coming from places on the hand.
rows.quote: microstimulation within the hand area of the somatosensory cortex of a person with long-term spinal cord injury evokes tactile sensations perceived as originating from locations on the hand
rows.citation: Flesher et al. (2016). Intracortical microstimulation of human somatosensory cortex. Sci Transl Med.
rows.study_design: single-participant intracortical microstimulation study
rows.scope_note: One participant with spinal cord injury. A stimulation effect; it is not evidence about what damage to this cortex does, and says nothing about astereognosis or phantom limb pain.
rows.anatomy_as_stated: hand area of the somatosensory cortex
rows.anatomy_note: equal or larger: the paper says 'hand area of the somatosensory cortex'; the abstract does not say 'primary'.

rows.claim: Drawing on three post-mortem cases, the earlier patient R.B. and other amnesic patients, the authors conclude that bilateral damage limited primarily to the CA1 field of the hippocampal formation is sufficient to produce moderately severe anterograde memory impairment.
rows.quote: Bilateral damage limited primarily to the CA1 region of the hippocampal formation is sufficient to produce moderately severe anterograde memory impairment.
rows.citation: Rempel-Clower et al. (1996). Three cases of enduring memory impairment after bilateral damage limited to the hippocampal formation. J Neurosci.
rows.study_design: neuropsychological and post-mortem neuropathological case series
rows.scope_note: Three patients plus the earlier patient R.B. The paper's word is 'sufficient', a claim the authors make from histology in a handful of cases. Says nothing about Alzheimer's disease, stress or PTSD.
rows.anatomy_as_stated: CA1 region of the hippocampal formation
rows.anatomy_note: part: the paper says 'the CA1 region of the hippocampal formation'.

rows.claim: In one patient (R.B.) with memory impairment after an ischaemic episode, post-mortem study found a bilateral lesion of hippocampal field CA1, which the authors judged the only damage reasonably associated with the memory defect.
rows.quote: the only damage that could be reasonably associated with the memory defect was the lesion in the hippocampus
rows.citation: Zola-Morgan et al. (1986). Human amnesia and the medial temporal region: enduring memory impairment following a bilateral lesion limited to field CA1 of the hippocampus. J Neurosci.
rows.study_design: single case, neuropsychological follow-up over 5 years and post-mortem histology
rows.scope_note: One patient. Minor pathology was also found elsewhere in the brain, as the abstract states.
rows.anatomy_note: part: the paper says 'the entire CA1 field of the hippocampus'.

rows.claim: Five people with selective bilateral damage to the basolateral amygdala, unlike matched controls, did not adjust their investments in a repeated trust game when dealing with a trustworthy and an untrustworthy partner.
rows.quote: BLA-damaged subjects, unlike control subjects, completely failed to adapt their investments when interacting with a trustworthy and an untrustworthy partner
rows.citation: Rosenberger et al. (2019). The Human Basolateral Amygdala Is Indispensable for Social Experiential Learning. Curr Biol.
rows.study_design: lesion group of five compared with matched healthy controls on a repeated trust game and a non-social task
rows.scope_note: Five people with a rare selective lesion (cause not in the abstract). Concerns learning from social experience in one task; it is not evidence about fear recognition, PTSD, anxiety or psychopathy.
rows.anatomy_note: equal: the paper says 'basolateral amygdala (BLA)'.

rows.claim: In one patient with selective bilateral amygdala damage, the findings suggested the amygdala may be needed to recognise fear in facial expressions.
rows.quote: we report findings that suggest the human amygdala may be indispensable to: (1) recognize fear in facial expressions
rows.citation: Adolphs et al. (1994). Impaired recognition of emotion in facial expressions following bilateral damage to the human amygdala. Nature.
rows.study_design: single-case lesion study
rows.scope_note: One patient. The lesion is of the amygdala as a whole, not the basolateral nuclei alone, so this cannot be attributed to the QIF sub-region. The authors hedge with 'suggest' and 'may be'.
rows.anatomy_note: larger: the paper says 'the human amygdala' and 'bilateral damage to the human amygdala'; the QIF region is the basolateral part only.

rows.claim: Smokers whose brain damage involved the insula were more likely than smokers with damage elsewhere to stop smoking easily, at once, without relapse and without a lasting urge to smoke.
rows.quote: smokers with brain damage involving the insula, a region implicated in conscious urges, were more likely than smokers with brain damage not involving the insula to undergo a disruption of smoking addiction
rows.citation: Naqvi et al. (2007). Damage to the insula disrupts addiction to cigarette smoking. Science.
rows.study_design: retrospective comparison of smokers with brain lesions involving or sparing the insula; numbers not in the abstract
rows.scope_note: 'More likely', a group comparison: it does not say insula damage ends craving in every patient. Sample size is not in the abstract. Retrospective. Damage 'involving' the insula may extend beyond it. Replication is mixed: a prospective study of 87 smokers with first-ever ischaemic stroke found no association between insular lesions and smoking status at three months (Bienkowski et al. 2010, PMID 20470864).
rows.anatomy_note: equal or larger: the paper says 'brain damage involving the insula'.

related_sources.citation: Bienkowski et al. (2010). Insular lesions and smoking cessation after first-ever ischemic stroke: a 3-month follow-up. Neurosci Lett.
related_sources.quote: Concluding, post-stroke smoking cessation may not be associated with insular lesions.

rows.claim: Across 4160 intracerebral stimulations in 164 patients being assessed for epilepsy surgery, pain responses were rare (1.4%) and were concentrated in the medial parietal operculum and neighbouring posterior insula.
rows.quote: Pain responses were scarce (1.4%) and concentrated in the medial part of the parietal operculum and neighbouring posterior insula where pain thresholds showed a rostrocaudal decrement.
rows.citation: Mazzola et al. (2012). Stimulation of the human cortex and the experience of pain: Wilder Penfield's observations revisited. Brain.
rows.study_design: retrospective analysis of intracerebral stimulation responses over 12 years, 164 consecutive patients, 4160 stimulations
rows.scope_note: One centre, epilepsy patients, electrode sites chosen for clinical reasons. Concerns the posterior insula together with the parietal operculum; it does not support statements about the anterior insula, disgust or empathy.
rows.anatomy_as_stated: medial part of the parietal operculum and neighbouring posterior insula
rows.anatomy_note: part plus a neighbour: the paper says 'the medial part of the parietal operculum and neighbouring posterior insula'.

rows.claim: Of 44 patients who had one or more cingulotomies for treatment-refractory obsessive-compulsive disorder, 14 met response criteria and 6 more were partial responders at a mean of 32 months.
rows.quote: At mean follow-up of 32 months after one or more cingulotomies, 14 patients (32%) met criteria for treatment response and six others (14%) were partial responders.
rows.citation: Dougherty et al. (2002). Prospective long-term follow-up of 44 patients who received cingulotomy for treatment-refractory obsessive-compulsive disorder. Am J Psychiatry.
rows.study_design: open prospective follow-up, no control group
rows.scope_note: Open study with no control group, one centre, highly selected patients. A surgical lesion in people with severe illness: it shows an association with improvement in some, and is not evidence about what the region does in health. Research summary, not treatment advice. The abstract never says 'anterior' or 'cortex'; the link to this region rests on the name of the operation.
rows.anatomy_as_stated: cingulotomy; the abstract names the operation and no brain structure
rows.anatomy_note: equal by the name of the operation, not stated in words: the abstract says 'cingulotomy' and never 'anterior cingulate cortex'.

rows.claim: A systematic review of 11 observational reports (224 patients) found that more than 60% of patients were reported to have significant pain relief after anterior cingulotomy, both after surgery and at one year.
rows.quote: Greater than 60% of patients across all studies were reported to have significant pain relief post-operatively as well as at one year after surgery.
rows.citation: Sharim and Pouratian (2016). Anterior Cingulotomy for the Treatment of Chronic Intractable Pain: A Systematic Review. Pain Physician.
rows.study_design: systematic review of observational studies
rows.scope_note: All included studies were observational and heterogeneous, as the review's own limitations state. No DOI is recorded in PubMed for this article. Research summary, not treatment advice.
rows.anatomy_note: equal by the name of the operation: the paper says 'anterior cingulotomy' and lists 'cingulate gyrus' as a key word.

rows.claim: Three patients with small haemorrhages extending from the right retrosplenial region to the medial parietal lobe had selective topographic disorientation.
rows.quote: We report three patients with selective topographic disorientation due to small, focal hemorrhages extending from the right retrosplenial region to the medial parietal lobe.
rows.citation: Takahashi et al. (1997). Pure topographic disorientation due to right retrosplenial lesion. Neurology.
rows.study_design: case series
rows.scope_note: Three patients, right-sided lesions that also reached the medial parietal lobe. Says nothing about the default mode network, Alzheimer's disease or anaesthesia.
rows.anatomy_as_stated: right retrosplenial region to the medial parietal lobe
rows.anatomy_note: part or neighbour: the paper says 'right retrosplenial region' and 'medial parietal lobe'; whether QIF's 'Cingulate Gyrus (Posterior)' includes retrosplenial cortex is a crosswalk decision still open in the build spec.

rows.claim: A review of published case reports of relatively pure topographical disorientation with a retrosplenial lesion found that all of those patients had impaired learning of new routes and defective navigation in familiar places, and that the deficit generally resolved within eight weeks.
rows.quote: All patients displayed impaired learning of new routes, and defective navigation in familiar environments complaining they could not use preserved landmark recognition to aid orientation.
rows.citation: Maguire (2001). The retrosplenial contribution to human navigation: a review of lesion and neuroimaging findings. Scand J Psychol.
rows.study_design: narrative review of lesion case reports and neuroimaging studies; number of cases not in the abstract
rows.scope_note: Review of case reports; the number of cases is not in the abstract. Most cases were right-sided. The recovery within eight weeks is stated in the next sentence of the abstract, not in the quote.
rows.anatomy_note: part or neighbour: the paper says 'retrosplenial cortex' and 'Brodmann's area 30'.

rows.claim: In a review of 240 published patients with focal basal ganglia lesions, lesions of the lentiform nucleus were commonly associated with dystonia (49%), more so when the putamen was involved (63%), and rarely with abulia (10%).
rows.quote: Lesions of the lentiform nuclei rarely caused abulia (10%) and did not produce disinhibition, but they commonly caused dystonia (49%), particularly when the putamen was involved (63%).
rows.citation: Bhatia and Marsden (1994). The behavioural and motor consequences of focal lesions of the basal ganglia in man. Brain.
rows.study_design: analysis of 240 case reports from the literature
rows.scope_note: Published case reports, so subject to reporting bias; imaging quality varied. The lentiform nucleus includes the globus pallidus, which is not part of the striatum. Focal lesions, not Parkinson's or Huntington's disease.
rows.anatomy_as_stated: lentiform nuclei (putamen and globus pallidus); putamen
rows.anatomy_note: part plus a neighbour: the paper says 'lentiform nuclei' (putamen and globus pallidus) and 'putamen'.

rows.claim: In the same review of 240 published patients, the most significant behavioural disturbance with caudate lesions was abulia, described in 28%.
rows.quote: The most significant behavioural disturbance described in 28% of those with caudate lesions was the syndrome of abulia, sometimes alternating with disinhibition (11%).
rows.citation: Bhatia and Marsden (1994). The behavioural and motor consequences of focal lesions of the basal ganglia in man. Brain.
rows.study_design: analysis of 240 case reports from the literature
rows.scope_note: Published case reports, so subject to reporting bias. The same abstract says caudate lesions rarely caused motor disorders, which limits any motor claim about the caudate.
rows.anatomy_note: part: the paper says 'caudate lesions'.

rows.claim: In a randomised sham-controlled trial in 40 patients with primary generalised or segmental dystonia, three months of bilateral pallidal stimulation was more effective than sham stimulation.
rows.quote: Bilateral pallidal neurostimulation for 3 months was more effective than sham stimulation in patients with primary generalized or segmental dystonia.
rows.citation: Kupsch et al. (2006). Pallidal deep-brain stimulation in primary generalized or segmental dystonia. N Engl J Med.
rows.study_design: randomised, sham-controlled trial with blinded video rating
rows.scope_note: A treatment effect of stimulation in people with dystonia; it does not show what the nucleus does in health and says nothing about Parkinson's disease or hemiballismus. Research summary, not treatment advice.
rows.anatomy_note: equal: the abstract's background says 'internal globus pallidus'; the conclusion says 'pallidal'.

rows.claim: In an open trial of bilateral stimulation of the external globus pallidus in 13 patients with refractory Tourette syndrome, the reported responder rate for tics was 76.9%.
rows.quote: Responder rates were 76.9%, 75%, 71.4%, 71.4%, and 85.7%, respectively, for TS, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), depression, anxiety, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.
rows.citation: Vilela-Filho et al. (2024). Bilateral Globus Pallidus Externus Deep Brain Stimulation for the Treatment of Refractory Tourette Syndrome: An Open Clinical Trial. Neuromodulation.
rows.study_design: open, uncontrolled clinical trial
rows.scope_note: Thirteen patients, no control group, no blinding, one group testing its own hypothesis. Not replicated in anything read here. It is not evidence for the indirect-pathway account in the atlas text. Research summary, not treatment advice.
rows.anatomy_note: equal: the paper says 'globus pallidus externus (GPe)'.

rows.claim: In a six-month randomised trial of 156 patients under 75 with advanced Parkinson's disease, stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus plus medication was more effective than medication alone on quality-of-life and motor scores; serious adverse events were more common with stimulation (13% versus 4%).
rows.quote: In this six-month study of patients under 75 years of age with severe motor complications of Parkinson's disease, neurostimulation of the subthalamic nucleus was more effective than medical management alone.
rows.citation: Deuschl et al. (2006). A randomized trial of deep-brain stimulation for Parkinson's disease. N Engl J Med.
rows.study_design: randomised-pairs trial, stimulation plus medication versus medication alone
rows.scope_note: Six months, patients under 75 with severe motor complications. Serious adverse events were more common with stimulation (13% versus 4%), including one fatal haemorrhage. The abstract gives no figure for medication dose reduction. Research summary, not treatment advice.
rows.anatomy_note: equal: the paper says 'subthalamic nucleus'.

rows.claim: A review of hemiballism reports that, against traditional teaching, the subthalamic nucleus is directly involved in only a minority of cases.
rows.quote: review of more recent reports shows that the STN is directly involved in only a minority of cases
rows.citation: Postuma and Lang (2003). Hemiballism: revisiting a classic disorder. Lancet Neurol.
rows.study_design: narrative review
rows.scope_note: Narrative review with no pooled numbers in the abstract. It limits the claim 'a subthalamic lesion gives hemiballismus': it does not deny that such lesions can be followed by hemiballism, only that hemiballism points to this nucleus.
rows.anatomy_note: equal: the paper says 'subthalamic nucleus (STN)'.

rows.claim: In a post-mortem study, 20 Parkinson's disease cases showed an exponential loss of pigmented neurons in the pars compacta of the caudal substantia nigra, with a 45% loss in the first decade of disease.
rows.quote: In 20 Parkinson's disease (PD) cases of varying disease duration there was an exponential loss of pigmented neurons with a 45% loss in the first decade.
rows.citation: Fearnley and Lees (1991). Ageing and Parkinson's disease: substantia nigra regional selectivity. Brain.
rows.study_design: post-mortem cell counts on one section per case; 36 controls, 20 Parkinson's disease, other parkinsonian groups
rows.scope_note: One stained section per case at one level of the caudal nigra. Cell loss is a correlate of the disease in tissue, not a lesion experiment.
rows.anatomy_as_stated: pars compacta of the caudal substantia nigra
rows.anatomy_note: part: the paper says 'pars compacta of the caudal substantia nigra'.

rows.claim: The same post-mortem study calculated that when Parkinson's symptoms begin there is about a 68% loss of pigmented cells in the lateral ventral tier and a 48% loss in the caudal nigra as a whole.
rows.quote: It was calculated that at the onset of symptoms there was a 68% cell loss in the lateral ventral tier and a 48% loss in the caudal nigra as a whole.
rows.citation: Fearnley and Lees (1991). Ageing and Parkinson's disease: substantia nigra regional selectivity. Brain.
rows.study_design: post-mortem cell counts on one section per case; the onset figures are an extrapolation
rows.scope_note: A calculated estimate from a regression over 20 cases, not a measurement at symptom onset. One section per case.
rows.anatomy_as_stated: lateral ventral tier; caudal nigra as a whole
rows.anatomy_note: part: the paper says 'lateral ventral tier' of the pars compacta and 'caudal nigra as a whole'.

rows.claim: In an uncontrolled open-label study of 21 patients with medically refractory chronic cluster headache, deep brain stimulation at a target the authors call the ventral tegmental area was followed by a 60% improvement in headache frequency at final follow-up.
rows.quote: At the final follow-up point, there was 60% improvement in headache frequency (p = 0.007) and 30% improvement in headache severity (p = 0.001).
rows.citation: Akram et al. (2016). Ventral tegmental area deep brain stimulation for refractory chronic cluster headache. Neurology.
rows.study_design: uncontrolled, open-label prospective cohort; the abstract rates it Class IV evidence
rows.scope_note: No control group, no blinding, one centre. The authors call the target the ventral tegmental area; whether the stimulated tissue is the dopamine cell group the QIF record describes was not checked. It is not evidence about reward, motivation, depression, addiction, schizophrenia or ADHD. Research summary, not treatment advice. Deep brain stimulation targets for cluster headache were long described as hypothalamic; a tractography study of four earlier published targets reports that they 'localized in the midbrain tegmentum posterior to the hypothalamus' (Clelland et al. 2014, PMID 24133007). That study predates this one and does not examine its target. Nothing read shows that the dopamine cell group in the QIF record was what was stimulated. Do not show this row without this caveat.
rows.anatomy_as_stated: ventral tegmental area (VTA), the authors' name for their stimulation target
rows.anatomy_note: equal by the paper's label: 'ventral tegmental area (VTA)'.

related_sources.citation: Clelland et al. (2014). Common cerebral networks associated with distinct deep brain stimulation targets for cluster headache. Cephalalgia.
related_sources.relation: bears on where such targets lie
related_sources.quote: Despite being described as hypothalamic, the DBS targets localized in the midbrain tegmentum posterior to the hypothalamus.

rows.claim: A review of thalamic infarction describes strokes in the inferolateral territory as associated with loss of sensation, weakness and incoordination on the opposite side of the body, and with pain syndromes.
rows.quote: Inferolateral territory strokes produce contralateral hemisensory loss, hemiparesis and hemiataxia, and pain syndromes that are more common after right thalamic lesions.
rows.citation: Schmahmann (2003). Vascular syndromes of the thalamus. Stroke.
rows.study_design: narrative review
rows.scope_note: Narrative review by one author, no pooled numbers. The syndrome depends on which arterial territory and nuclei are hit, so it is not a property of 'the thalamus' as a whole.
rows.anatomy_note: part: the paper says 'inferolateral territory' of the thalamus.

rows.claim: The same review describes paramedian thalamic infarcts as associated with decreased arousal, particularly when bilateral, and with impaired learning and memory.
rows.quote: Paramedian infarcts cause decreased arousal, particularly if the lesion is bilateral, and impaired learning and memory.
rows.citation: Schmahmann (2003). Vascular syndromes of the thalamus. Stroke.
rows.study_design: narrative review
rows.scope_note: Narrative review by one author, no pooled numbers. One vascular territory only.
rows.anatomy_note: part: the paper says 'paramedian' thalamic territory.

rows.claim: In a prospective cohort of 709 children with craniopharyngioma, posterior hypothalamic involvement and hypothalamic lesion were independent risk factors for obesity at last visit and for reduced event-free survival.
rows.quote: Posterior hypothalamic involvement and hypothalamic lesion (HL) were independent risk factors for reduced EFS (hazard ratio = 1.59, 95% CI [1.12-2.26]) and obesity at last visit (odds ratio = 2.94, 95% CI [1.73-5.08]).
rows.citation: Beckhaus et al. (2023). Outcome after pediatric craniopharyngioma: the role of age at diagnosis and hypothalamic damage. Eur J Endocrinol.
rows.study_design: prospective registry cohort
rows.scope_note: Children with one tumour type and its treatment; tumour, surgery and radiotherapy effects are not separable in the abstract. A risk factor in a cohort, not an individual prediction. Says nothing about puberty, diabetes insipidus, temperature, narcolepsy or Cushing's disease.
rows.anatomy_note: equal and part: the paper says 'hypothalamic lesion (HL)' and 'posterior hypothalamic involvement'.

rows.claim: In 32 patients with disabling tremor (26 with Parkinson's disease, 6 with essential tremor), high-frequency stimulation of the ventral intermediate nucleus gave complete relief from tremor in 27 of 43 stimulated thalami and major improvement in 11.
rows.quote: Of the 43 thalami stimulated, 27 showed complete relief from tremor and 11 major improvement (88%).
rows.citation: Benabid et al. (1991). Long-term suppression of tremor by chronic stimulation of the ventral intermediate thalamic nucleus. Lancet.
rows.study_design: uncontrolled case series, tremor measured by accelerometry
rows.scope_note: Uncontrolled 1991 series, mostly Parkinson's disease; only 6 patients had essential tremor. The 88% counts thalami, not patients, and is not a percentage reduction in tremor. Research summary, not treatment advice.
rows.anatomy_note: equal: the paper says 'ventral intermediate nucleus (Vim)'.

rows.claim: In a randomised sham-controlled trial analysing 76 patients with essential tremor, a focused ultrasound lesion in the thalamus (the abstract names no nucleus) reduced hand tremor, with sensory and gait disturbances as side effects.
rows.quote: MRI-guided focused ultrasound thalamotomy reduced hand tremor in patients with essential tremor. Side effects included sensory and gait disturbances.
rows.citation: Elias et al. (2016). A Randomized Trial of Focused Ultrasound Thalamotomy for Essential Tremor. N Engl J Med.
rows.study_design: randomised, sham-controlled trial (3:1), blinded video rating
rows.scope_note: The abstract says 'thalamotomy' and never names the nucleus targeted, so on the text read this supports 'a lesion in the thalamus', not 'a lesion in the ventral intermediate nucleus'. Paresthesias or numbness occurred in 38% and persisted at 12 months in 14%. Research summary, not treatment advice. Show as 'thalamus' until a full text naming the target is read; no open full text was found for this paper.
rows.anatomy_as_stated: thalamus (the abstract says 'thalamotomy' and names no nucleus)
rows.anatomy_note: larger: the paper says 'unilateral focused ultrasound thalamotomy'; the nucleus is not named in the abstract.

rows.claim: In a multicentre double-blind randomised trial of 110 adults with medically refractory partial seizures, the group receiving bilateral stimulation of the anterior nuclei of the thalamus had a 29% greater reduction in seizures than the control group in the last month of the blinded phase.
rows.quote: In the last month of the blinded phase the stimulated group had a 29% greater reduction in seizures compared with the control group, as estimated by a generalized estimating equations (GEE) model (p = 0.002).
rows.citation: Fisher et al. (2010). Electrical stimulation of the anterior nucleus of thalamus for treatment of refractory epilepsy. Epilepsia.
rows.study_design: multicentre, double-blind, randomised trial with a 3-month blinded phase and open-label follow-up
rows.scope_note: The blinded comparison lasted three months; the 56% median reduction at two years comes from the unblinded phase with no control group. Participants in the stimulated group were more likely to report depression or memory problems. Research summary, not treatment advice.
rows.anatomy_note: equal: the paper says 'anterior nuclei of the thalamus'.

rows.claim: In a post-mortem comparison of alcoholics with and without amnesia, neuronal loss in the anterior thalamic nuclei was found consistently only in those with Korsakoff's psychosis.
rows.quote: neuronal loss in the anterior thalamic nuclei was found consistently only in alcoholic Korsakoff's psychosis
rows.citation: Harding et al. (2000). Degeneration of anterior thalamic nuclei differentiates alcoholics with amnesia. Brain.
rows.study_design: post-mortem stereological neuron counts in amnesic and non-amnesic alcoholics; group sizes not in the abstract
rows.scope_note: Group sizes are not in the abstract. Mamillary and mediodorsal nuclei were damaged in both groups, so the finding is about what differs between groups, not about the only site of damage. Post-mortem association.
rows.anatomy_note: equal: the paper says 'anterior thalamic nuclei'.

rows.claim: In a lesion-mapping study of 90 patients with focal cerebellar lesions, upper limb ataxia was correlated with lesions of lobules IV-V and VI in the vermis, paravermis and hemisphere; the authors report that correlations with cortical lesions were less significant than those with nuclear lesions.
rows.quote: Upper limb ataxia was correlated with lesions of vermal, paravermal and hemispheral lobules IV-V and VI
rows.citation: Schoch et al. (2006). Functional localization in the human cerebellum based on voxelwise statistical analysis: a study of 90 patients. Neuroimage.
rows.study_design: voxel-based lesion-symptom mapping; 43 ischaemic and 47 surgical lesions
rows.scope_note: The same abstract says correlations with cortical lesions were less significant than those with nuclear lesions and were present in the superior cerebellum only. Group statistics, strongest in the acute ischaemic subgroup.
rows.anatomy_as_stated: vermal, paravermal and hemispheral lobules IV-V and VI
rows.anatomy_note: part: the paper says 'cerebellar cortex' and names lobules IV-V and VI.

rows.claim: In 20 patients with disease confined to the cerebellum, behavioural changes were clinically prominent in those whose lesions involved the posterior lobe and the vermis.
rows.quote: Behavioural changes were clinically prominent in patients with lesions involving the posterior lobe of the cerebellum and the vermis, and in some cases they were the most noticeable aspects of the presentation.
rows.citation: Schmahmann and Sherman (1998). The cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome. Brain.
rows.study_design: case series with neurological, bedside and neuropsychological testing and anatomical imaging
rows.scope_note: Twenty patients, one centre, mixed causes. Lesions are described by lobe; the abstract does not separate cortex from white matter or nuclei, so this cannot be pinned on the cerebellar cortex or on Purkinje cells. Uncontrolled series. A controlled study of 32 adults with focal cerebellar stroke or tumour resection concluded that such impairment 'is mild or transient' (Alexander et al. 2012, PMID 21549360).
rows.anatomy_as_stated: posterior lobe of the cerebellum and the vermis
rows.anatomy_note: larger: the paper says 'the posterior lobe of the cerebellum and the vermis'.

related_sources.citation: Alexander et al. (2012). Cognitive impairments due to focal cerebellar injuries in adults. Cortex.
related_sources.quote: the cognitive impairment after focal cerebellar injury in adults is mild or transient

rows.claim: In a lesion-mapping study of 90 patients with focal cerebellar lesions, limb ataxia was correlated with lesions of the interposed and part of the dentate nuclei, and ataxia of posture and gait with lesions of the fastigial nuclei.
rows.quote: Limb ataxia was significantly correlated with lesions of the interposed (NI) and part of the dentate nuclei (ND), ataxia of posture and gait with lesions of the fastigial nuclei (NF) including NI.
rows.citation: Schoch et al. (2006). Functional localization in the human cerebellum based on voxelwise statistical analysis: a study of 90 patients. Neuroimage.
rows.study_design: voxel-based lesion-symptom mapping; 43 ischaemic and 47 surgical lesions
rows.scope_note: Group statistics, most significant in the acute ischaemic subgroup. The abstract does not mention intention tremor, dysmetria or cognitive and affective changes.
rows.anatomy_note: equal: the paper says 'cerebellar nuclei' and names the interposed, dentate and fastigial nuclei.

rows.claim: In a lesion-mapping study of 90 patients with focal cerebellar lesions, ataxia of posture and gait was correlated with lesions of vermal and paravermal lobules II, III and IV; the authors report that correlations with cortical lesions were less significant than those with nuclear lesions.
rows.quote: ataxia of posture and gait with lesions of vermal and paravermal lobules II, III and IV
rows.citation: Schoch et al. (2006). Functional localization in the human cerebellum based on voxelwise statistical analysis: a study of 90 patients. Neuroimage.
rows.study_design: voxel-based lesion-symptom mapping; 43 ischaemic and 47 surgical lesions
rows.scope_note: The quote is the last clause of a long sentence whose verb ('was correlated with') comes earlier in that sentence. Anterior vermis and paravermis only. Group statistics.
rows.anatomy_as_stated: vermal and paravermal lobules II, III and IV
rows.anatomy_note: part plus a neighbour: the paper says 'vermal and paravermal lobules II, III and IV'.

rows.claim: A 2022 meta-analysis of 28 studies (2276 children) listed a surgical incision through the vermis among the univariate risk factors for postoperative cerebellar mutism syndrome (odds ratio 5.44); a 2026 pooled review of 16 studies found no significant difference between transvermian and telovelar approaches.
rows.quote: a vermis incision (OR 5.44, 95% CI 2.09-14.16; p = 0.0005)
rows.citation: Pettersson et al. (2022). Risk factors for postoperative cerebellar mutism syndrome in pediatric patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Neurosurg Pediatr.
rows.study_design: systematic review and meta-analysis of comparative studies in patients aged 18 or under
rows.scope_note: Univariate analysis; the authors note that risk factors may depend on one another (tumour type, size and location were also significant). Children having tumour surgery only. The quote is one item from a list whose lead-in ('Statistically significant risk factors identified from univariate analysis were') comes earlier in the same sentence. The 2026 pooled review is Egeborg et al. (PMID 42569686): 16 studies, 1369 patients, pooled odds ratio 1.85 (95% CI 0.95 to 3.59). It compares two surgical routes, which is not the same question as the 2022 univariate factor.
rows.anatomy_note: equal: the paper says 'a vermis incision'.

related_sources.citation: Egeborg et al. (2026). Does the surgical route matter in cerebellar mutism syndrome? Comparing transvermian and telovelar approaches for pediatric posterior fossa tumors. Brain Spine.
related_sources.quote: We found no significant difference in CMS risk between transvermian and telovelar approaches, indicating no clear advantage of either approach in preventing CMS.

requires_citations.role: contrary pooled review; must be shown with the quoted paper

rows.claim: Among 130 consecutive patients with pure lateral medullary infarction, those with rostral lesions had difficulty swallowing, facial weakness and slurred speech more often, and severe gait ataxia and headache less often, than those with caudal lesions.
rows.quote: Patients with rostrally located lesions had dysphagia, facial paresis (P < 0.01, each) and dysarthria (P < 0.05) significantly more often, and severe gait ataxia and headache (P < 0.05, each) less often than those with caudal lesions.
rows.citation: Kim (2003). Pure lateral medullary infarction: clinical-radiological correlation of 130 acute, consecutive patients. Brain.
rows.study_design: consecutive case series with clinical and MRI correlation
rows.scope_note: One centre. Lateral medulla only. Compares lesion locations within the syndrome; gives no rates against people without medullary lesions. The abstract says nothing about breathing, the heart or death.
rows.anatomy_note: part: the paper says 'lateral medullary infarction'.

rows.claim: From two patients with one-sided infarcts of the caudal brainstem and central hypoventilation, the authors suggest that one-sided involvement of the pontomedullary reticular formation and nucleus ambiguus is enough to produce loss of automatic breathing.
rows.quote: We suggest that unilateral involvement of pontomedullary reticular formation and nucleus ambiguus is sufficient for generating loss of automatic respiration
rows.citation: Bogousslavsky et al. (1990). Respiratory failure and unilateral caudal brainstem infarction. Ann Neurol.
rows.study_design: two clinicopathological cases
rows.scope_note: Two patients. 'We suggest' is the authors' wording. The structures named lie within and next to the medulla; this row is also relevant to the reticular formation.
rows.anatomy_as_stated: pontomedullary reticular formation and nucleus ambiguus
rows.anatomy_note: part: the paper says 'pontomedullary reticular formation and nucleus ambiguus' and 'medullary reticular formation'.

rows.claim: Four patients with locked-in syndrome of vascular origin, in whom clinical and radiological features supported infarction of the ventral pons, made substantial recovery.
rows.quote: Four patients made substantial recovery following the locked-in syndrome of vascular origin. Clinical and radiologic features supported the presence of ventral pontine infarction secondary to basilar artery occlusion.
rows.citation: McCusker et al. (1982). Recovery from the 'locked-in' syndrome. Arch Neurol.
rows.study_design: case series
rows.scope_note: Four patients chosen because they recovered; the abstract itself says only 'a few patients' do. Lesion site 'supported' by 1982 clinical and radiological features, not proven. Does not address REM sleep or myelinolysis.
rows.anatomy_note: part: the paper says 'ventral pontine infarction'.

rows.claim: In two patients with locked-in syndrome, post-mortem examination found basilar artery thrombosis with infarction of the ventral rostral pons extending into the paramedian tegmental area.
rows.quote: Postmortem examination reveals in both cases a thrombosis of the basilar artery with an infarction of the ventral rostral pons extending dorsally into the paramedian tegmental area.
rows.citation: Dehaene and Martin (1976). "Locked-in" syndrome. A clinico-pathological study of two cases. Eur Neurol.
rows.study_design: two clinicopathological cases
rows.scope_note: Two patients. Shows where the lesion was in two people with the syndrome; cannot say how often a pontine stroke produces it.
rows.anatomy_as_stated: ventral rostral pons; paramedian tegmental area
rows.anatomy_note: part: the paper says 'ventral rostral pons' and 'paramedian tegmental area'.

rows.claim: Among 40 patients with infarcts limited to the midbrain, the commonest findings were gait ataxia (68%), slurred speech (55%) and limb ataxia (50%); third nerve palsy was seen in 35%.
rows.quote: Clinical manifestations included gait ataxia in 27 (68%) patients, dysarthria in 22 (55%), limb ataxia in 20 (50%), sensory symptoms in 17 (43%), third nerve palsy in 14 (35%)
rows.citation: Kim and Kim (2005). Pure midbrain infarction: clinical, radiologic, and pathophysiologic findings. Neurology.
rows.study_design: case series with MRI and angiography
rows.scope_note: One centre. The quote stops part-way through a list: the sentence goes on to give definite limb weakness in 9 (23%) and internuclear ophthalmoplegia in 5 (13%). The abstract does not use the names Weber or Parinaud and does not mention pain sensitivity.
rows.anatomy_note: equal: the paper says 'infarcts limited to the midbrain'.

rows.claim: In a retrospective MRI study of 47 patients with brainstem stroke, the 9 patients with coma had tegmental lesions that were mostly bilateral and lay in the pons alone or in the upper pons and midbrain.
rows.quote: patients who had coma (n = 9), the lesions in the tegmentum were mostly bilateral (n = 7) and were located either in the pons alone (n = 4) or in the upper pons and the midbrain (n = 5)
rows.citation: Parvizi and Damasio (2003). Neuroanatomical correlates of brainstem coma. Brain.
rows.study_design: retrospective lesion mapping on MRI, checked against charts and available post-mortem material
rows.scope_note: Nine coma patients. The paper localises to the brainstem tegmentum and to named nuclei within the overlap, not to 'the reticular formation' as one structure. Says nothing about narcolepsy, anaesthesia or brain death. The quote begins mid-sentence: the words 'In contrast, in' precede it in the abstract.
rows.anatomy_as_stated: brainstem tegmentum (pons alone, or upper pons and midbrain)
rows.anatomy_note: larger and overlapping: the paper says 'the brainstem tegmentum, including the reticular formation'.

rows.claim: Comparing 12 coma-causing brainstem lesions with 24 control brainstem lesions, a small region in the rostral dorsolateral pontine tegmentum was significantly associated with coma.
rows.quote: A small region in the rostral dorsolateral pontine tegmentum was significantly associated with coma-causing lesions.
rows.citation: Fischer et al. (2016). A human brain network derived from coma-causing brainstem lesions. Neurology.
rows.study_design: case-control voxel-based lesion-symptom mapping
rows.scope_note: Twelve cases. The site is a small part of the pontine tegmentum; the abstract does not call it the reticular formation.
rows.anatomy_note: part or overlapping, by the drafter's reading: the paper says 'rostral dorsolateral pontine tegmentum' and does not use the words reticular formation.

rows.claim: In four people diagnosed with complete paralysis of the legs after spinal cord injury, intentional leg movements occurred with epidural stimulation of the lumbosacral spinal cord; the authors attribute this to a change in the excitability of lumbosacral spinal networks.
rows.quote: neuromodulation of the sub-threshold motor state of excitability of the lumbosacral spinal networks was the key to recovery of intentional movement in four of four individuals diagnosed as having complete paralysis of the legs
rows.citation: Angeli et al. (2014). Altering spinal cord excitability enables voluntary movements after chronic complete paralysis in humans. Brain.
rows.study_design: case series of epidural stimulation after chronic spinal cord injury
rows.scope_note: Four people, one centre, no control condition described in the abstract. 'Was the key' is the authors' interpretation. The stimulation covered lumbosacral cord, so it cannot be assigned to lumbar segments alone, and it is a stimulation effect, not a statement about lumbar injury. Movement occurred with stimulation; the abstract does not report lasting recovery without it. A 2015 corrigendum added a conflict-of-interest statement.
rows.anatomy_note: larger: the paper says 'lumbosacral spinal networks'.

rows.claim: A meta-analysis of 322 patients with cauda equina syndrome from lumbar disc herniation found better recovery of sensory and motor deficits and of urinary and rectal function in those decompressed within 48 hours than in those decompressed later.
rows.quote: A significant improvement in sensory and motor deficits as well as urinary and rectal function occurred in patients who underwent decompression within 48 hours versus after 48 hours.
rows.citation: Ahn et al. (2000). Cauda equina syndrome secondary to lumbar disc herniation: a meta-analysis of surgical outcomes. Spine (Phila Pa 1976).
rows.study_design: meta-analysis of 42 reports
rows.scope_note: Pooled observational reports, not randomised. The same abstract found no difference between surgery within 24 hours and at 24 to 48 hours, and calls the timing of surgery controversial. It does not say deficits become permanent after 48 hours. Research summary, not medical advice. A published critique of this meta-analysis concluded that 'a flawed methodology and misinterpretation of results are reported, understating the value of early surgical intervention' (Kohles et al. 2004, PMID 15167669).
rows.anatomy_note: equal: the paper says 'cauda equina syndrome secondary to lumbar disc herniation'.

related_sources.citation: Kohles et al. (2004). Time-dependent surgical outcomes following cauda equina syndrome diagnosis: comments on a meta-analysis. Spine (Phila Pa 1976).
related_sources.quote: We conclude that a flawed methodology and misinterpretation of results are reported, understating the value of early surgical intervention.

rows.claim: In 80 patients studied within 24 hours of acute left-hemisphere stroke, the authors report that, among the 50 without infarct in Wernicke's area, word comprehension errors correlated strongly with delayed blood flow in that area, and they read this as further evidence that the area is crucial for word comprehension.
rows.quote: These results add further evidence for the crucial role of Wernicke's area (Brodmann's area 22) in word comprehension
rows.citation: Hillis et al. (2001). Hypoperfusion of Wernicke's area predicts severity of semantic deficit in acute stroke. Ann Neurol.
rows.study_design: prospective acute stroke series with diffusion and perfusion MRI and language tests; the correlation is in 50 of the 80 patients
rows.scope_note: CONTESTED TOPIC, recorded and not resolved. This is the classical side; the other two rows under this region argue against it. The measure is delayed perfusion, not a lesion, in the first day after stroke. A correlation; 'crucial role' is the authors' reading. Added in round 2 at the verifier's suggestion and not itself checked by the verifier.
rows.anatomy_note: The paper defines the area as Brodmann's area 22; Binder 2017 defines it as posterior superior temporal gyrus plus supramarginal gyrus. The two definitions differ.

rows.claim: Against the view that spatial neglect goes with posterior parietal lesions, the authors report that the superior temporal cortex, largely on the right, is the site associated with spatial neglect in humans.
rows.quote: Here we show that, contrary to the widely accepted view, the superior temporal cortex is the neural substrate of spatial neglect in humans, as it is in monkeys.
rows.citation: Karnath et al. (2001). Spatial awareness is a function of the temporal not the posterior parietal lobe. Nature.
rows.study_design: lesion study in patients with spatial neglect; design and numbers are not in the abstract
rows.scope_note: CONTESTED TOPIC, recorded and not resolved. This is the rival to Mort et al. 2003 and it places the site OUTSIDE this region; it is filed here only so the dispute is visible. No sample size or method in the abstract. Added in round 2 at the verifier's suggestion and not itself checked by the verifier.
rows.anatomy_note: The paper says 'superior temporal cortex', which is not part of the posterior parietal cortex.

rows.claim: In 26 people with chronic spinal cord injury at T6 or above (15 cervical, 11 thoracic), those with cervical injury had lower ventilation and higher carbon dioxide during sleep than those with thoracic injury, which the authors suggest points to sleep-related hypoventilation.
rows.quote: Decreased VI and increased PETCO2 during sleep in patients with cervical SCI relative to thoracic SCI suggests that sleep related hypoventilation may contribute to the pathogenesis SDB in patients with chronic cervical SCI.
rows.citation: Sankari et al. (2014). Sleep disordered breathing in chronic spinal cord injury. J Clin Sleep Med.
rows.study_design: consecutive case series with spirometry and attended polysomnography, comparing injury levels
rows.scope_note: Fifteen cervical and eleven thoracic patients, one centre, none on a ventilator. 'Suggests' and 'may contribute' are the authors' words. An injury at a level also cuts everything below it, so this is about cervical-level injury, not about what cervical segments do. Says nothing about arm function or named cord syndromes. Replaces a round-1 row the verifier dropped; not itself checked by the verifier. Crossref lists a publisher erratum to this article (doi 10.5664/jcsm.4054, 2014); its content was not read, it is not a retraction, and PubMed shows no notice. The abstract gives no test statistic for the cervical versus thoracic comparison.
rows.anatomy_as_stated: cervical SCI (spinal cord injury at a cervical level)
rows.anatomy_note: Equal by level: the paper says 'cervical SCI' and compares it with 'thoracic SCI'.

empty_regions.reason: No human lesion or stimulation study found whose abstract ties a deficit to the thoracic cord itself. The one lead read (Lee et al. 2017, PMID 29226126, 28 patients) concerns injuries 'above T6', which includes cervical injuries, so it was not used.
empty_regions.name: Thoracic Spinal Cord

empty_regions.reason: No human lesion or stimulation study found whose abstract names the sacral cord and a deficit. A systematic review of conus medullaris and cauda equina definitions (Brouwers et al. 2017, PMID 28534496) defines the syndromes by level but reports no deficit data in its abstract. One of the searches for this region returned nothing.
empty_regions.name: Sacral Spinal Cord

empty_regions.reason: Only animal evidence found for the central nucleus specifically. Human amygdala lesion studies read this session concern the whole amygdala or the basolateral part and are filed under bla.
empty_regions.name: Central Amygdala
